justification_text:
My point estimates were anchored primarily to the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, with relatively modest directional drift assumed across all three horizons. For the one-day estimate, I leaned heavily on short-term momentum and mean-reversion tendencies, essentially expecting prices to remain close to where they were with only minor fluctuation. For the one-week estimate, I applied a slight downward nudge to reflect the natural uncertainty that accumulates over several trading sessions and the possibility of modest consolidation after any recent moves. For the one-month estimate, the point estimate drifted only marginally lower, reflecting my baseline assumption of a roughly range-bound or slowly drifting environment rather than a strong directional trend. In all three cases, I was not embedding a strong bullish or bearish macro view, so the estimates cluster tightly around the starting level.

The confidence interval widths reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At the one-day horizon, the interval is relatively narrow because intraday and overnight price moves for most liquid assets tend to be bounded absent a shock. By the one-week horizon, the interval widens meaningfully to account for the accumulation of daily volatility, news flow, and the possibility of a momentum shift. At the one-month horizon, the interval widens further still, capturing the realistic range of outcomes when multiple weeks of trading, macro data releases, and sentiment shifts are all in play. The widths are calibrated to roughly reflect historical realized volatility at each time horizon rather than any specific event risk.

There are several risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected macro data print, a surprise policy easing signal, or a broad risk-on sentiment shift could drive prices well above the upper bound, particularly at the one-month horizon where the tail is thicker. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in economic conditions, a geopolitical shock, or a liquidity event could easily breach the lower bound of the confidence interval. These fat-tail risks are always present and are perhaps underrepresented even in my wider one-month interval, since truly extreme events by definition fall in the tails that 90% confidence intervals are designed to exclude.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume relatively stable volatility regimes. If market volatility itself were to spike, as it does during crises or major surprises, both the point estimates and interval widths could shift dramatically. Regime changes, such as a pivot in central bank policy or a sudden repricing of credit risk, represent the class of event most likely to render these forecasts poorly calibrated, since they can simultaneously shift the mean and widen the distribution in ways that historical volatility estimates do not fully anticipate.
